newsitem.title: TAJIKISTAN: Tajik leader pledges to free hostages, reporters.
newsitem.headline: Tajik leader pledges to free hostages, reporters.

text.p: Tajik President Imomali Rakhmonov pledged on Thursday to free groups of journalists and U.N. military observers captured by Tajik rebels earlier this week and said negotiations would start immediately.
"The president held an urgent meeting of the government this morning," spokesman Zafar Saidov said. "He gave them the task of freeing hostages today by peaceful means."
Saidov said Rakhmonov had ordered General Gafar Mirzoyev, head of his presidential guard, to start negotiations with the rebels, who are led by Rizvon Sadirov.

"Mirzoyev has already left for the area controlled by Sadirov's men to start talks on the release of hostages," Saidov said. "The president told the government meeting that there is no threat to the life of the hostages at the moment."

Sadirov's group, which once fought for Tajikistan's Islamic opposition against the secular government but whose loyalties are now unclear, has captured four members of the United Nations Mission of Observers in Tajikistan (UNMOT), four Russian journalists and two Red Cross workers in the last few days.

The rebels are demanding safe passage for members of the group based in neighbouring Afghanistan back into the former Soviet republic, an impoverished, mountainous country which also borders China, Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan.

The U.N. mission in Tajikistan issued a statement on Wednesday demanding "immediate and unconditional" release of all hostages, and the U.S.-based Committee to Protect Journalists asked Rakhmonov to do everything he could to help.

"CPJ urges you to seek the immediate release and safe passage of the four journalists and to guarantee safe and free working conditions for journalists covering the conflict in Tajikistan," it said in a letter to Rakhmonov distributed to news organisations.
The four reporters work for two Russian news agencies and for NTV commercial television. The captured UNMOT observers are from Austria, Ukraine, Switzerland and Tajikistan.
Saidov said it had been hard to guarantee the safety of people who travelled in Tajikistan without telling the authorities where they were going.

"The president noted with regret that the representatives of the international organisations and the journalists provided no information on the route of their missions, as it should be the rule," he said.
"Under the circumstances, it was difficult for the government to safeguard their security."
Foreign diplomats in the Tajik capital Dushanbe say that Rakhmonov controls only 15 to 20 percent of Tajik territory.
Tens of thousands of people were killed and many more made homeless during a four-year civil war in Tajikistan.
But a ceasefire agreed between the government and the guerrillas has held for nearly two months and further peace talks are due to be held on February 26 in Moscow.
Last December, Sadyrov's group took 23 people hostage, including seven U.N. observers, to demand the release of his brother. All the hostages were later released.
